entry.title: Making a valid will in India: what you actually need

link.title: Making a valid will in India: what you actually need

entry.content:
Many people put off writing a will because they assume it’s complicated or expensive. In most cases it is neither. What matters is getting a few formalities right, because a will is only tested after you’re gone, when you can no longer explain what you meant.

This article covers wills under the Indian Succession Act, 1925, which applies to most people in India. Muslims are largely governed by their personal law, under which a person generally can’t leave more than one-third of their estate by will without the consent of the heirs.

Who can make a will?

Anyone who is an adult (18 or above) and of sound mind at the time of making it. The will speaks from the date of death, but the mental capacity is judged at the date it was signed.

The three formalities that matter

Section 63 of the Act sets out how a will must be executed:

  1. It must be in writing. Typed or handwritten, in any language. There’s no prescribed format.
  2. You must sign it (or put your mark) in a way that shows you intend it to be your will.
  3. Two or more witnesses must attest it. Each witness must see you sign, and must sign in your presence.

That’s the core of it. A will that meets these three requirements is valid, even on plain paper.

Common myths

“It has to be on stamp paper.” No. There is no stamp duty on a will.

“It has to be registered.” No. Registration is optional. It does, however, make the will harder to challenge and keeps a safe copy with the Sub-Registrar, so it’s often worth doing.

“It has to be made by a lawyer.” No, though a lawyer can help you avoid ambiguity, which is the most common cause of disputes.

Don’t make a beneficiary your witness

This is the single most common mistake. Under Section 67, if a witness (or their spouse) is also a beneficiary, the gift to them is void. The rest of the will survives, but that person loses their share. Choose witnesses who receive nothing under the will.

Other things worth doing

  • Name an executor: a person you trust to carry out the will.
  • Describe property clearly: addresses, survey numbers, account and folio numbers.
  • Say what happens to anything you forgot, with a “residuary” clause.
  • Date every page and sign every page.
  • Keep it safe and tell someone where it is.
  • Review it after major life events: marriage, the birth of a child, a death in the family, or a large purchase.

Can I change it later?

Yes, as often as you like. You can make a fresh will (which should expressly revoke earlier ones) or add a codicil, a short document that amends the will and is executed with the same formalities. The last valid will is the one that counts.

Will my family need probate?

Probate is a court’s certification of a will. It’s compulsory only in certain cases, chiefly wills made by Hindus, Buddhists, Sikhs and Jains within the original areas of Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata, or dealing with immovable property there. Elsewhere it’s usually optional, though banks and housing societies sometimes ask for it.

The short version: write it down, sign it, have two independent witnesses sign in front of you, and consider registering it. That’s most of what you need.
entry.summary: No stamp paper, no compulsory registration, and no lawyer required. But there are a few rules you can't skip.

entry.title: Your cheque bounced. Here’s exactly what to do, and by when.

link.title: Your cheque bounced. Here’s exactly what to do, and by when.

entry.content:
A returned cheque is one of the most common money disputes in India, and the law gives you a strong remedy. The catch is that the remedy runs on strict deadlines. Miss one and you may lose the criminal route entirely.

When does Section 138 apply?

Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 makes it an offence when a cheque is dishonoured because:

  • there wasn’t enough money in the account, or
  • the amount exceeded the arrangement the drawer had with the bank.

The cheque must have been given for a legally enforceable debt or liability. A cheque given as a gift, for example, won’t qualify. Once the cheque and signature are admitted, the law presumes it was given for a debt (Section 139). It’s then for the drawer to prove otherwise.

The timeline at a glance

Step Deadline
Present the cheque to your bank Within 3 months of the date on the cheque
Send a written demand notice to the drawer Within 30 days of the bank telling you it bounced
Drawer may pay Within 15 days of receiving your notice
File the complaint in court Within 1 month after those 15 days end

Step by step

1. Keep the return memo

Your bank will return the cheque with a memo stating the reason for dishonour. Keep the original cheque and the memo safe. They are your primary evidence.

2. Send a legal notice within 30 days

The notice must demand payment of the cheque amount. Send it by registered post with acknowledgement due (and, ideally, by courier and email too), and keep every receipt and tracking record.

3. Wait 15 days

If the drawer pays within 15 days of receiving the notice, the matter ends there. If they don’t, the offence is complete.

4. File the complaint within a month

The complaint is filed before the magistrate having jurisdiction where your bank branch (where you deposited the cheque) is located. If you miss this window, the court can condone the delay, but only if you show sufficient cause. Don’t rely on that.

What can the court do?

The drawer can be punished with imprisonment of up to two years, a fine of up to twice the cheque amount, or both. The court can also order the drawer to pay interim compensation of up to 20% of the cheque amount while the case is pending (Section 143A).

The offence is compoundable, which means the parties can settle at any stage, and many cases do.

Can I also file a civil suit?

Yes. The criminal complaint and a civil suit for recovery are separate remedies and can run side by side. A summary suit under Order XXXVII of the Code of Civil Procedure is often used for this.

Quick checklist

  • Original cheque and bank return memo
  • Copy of the demand notice
  • Postal receipts and delivery proof
  • Evidence of the underlying debt (agreement, invoices, messages, bank transfers)
  • A calendar with every deadline marked

The short version: act within 30 days of the bounce, keep every document, and speak to an advocate early. The deadlines are where most of these cases are won or lost.
entry.summary: A step-by-step guide to Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act: the notice, the deadlines, and the complaint.

entry.title: Why I’m starting this blog
entry.content:
Every week, someone asks me a legal question over a cup of tea. A friend about to sign a rent agreement. A cousin whose cheque was returned. A neighbour wondering whether a handwritten will is “valid”.

The questions are almost always good ones, and the answers are almost always simpler than people fear. But the answers are hard to find, buried in bare acts, long judgments and websites written by lawyers for other lawyers.

What this blog will do

Each article will take one real question and answer it in plain language:

  1. What the law says, with the actual section, so you can check it yourself.
  2. What it means in practice: the deadlines, the documents, the usual pitfalls.
  3. What you can do next, including when it’s time to speak to an advocate.

What it won’t do

It won’t give advice on your specific case. Law depends on facts, and two situations that look identical often aren’t. Treat these articles as a map, not a destination.

If there’s a question you’d like answered, write to me. I read every message.
entry.summary: Most legal problems grow in the dark. Here's what this blog is for, and what you can expect from it.
